q: 1. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Shear stress can act in both horizontal and vertical planes depending on the loading conditions and the orientation of the cross-section being analyzed.

q: 2. Elasticity of a body is
options: the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
explain: Elasticity represents the internal resistance of the material molecules to being separated by an external force.

q: 3. Strain energy of a member may be defined as work done on it
explain: Strain energy is the internal work stored in a material due to any form of deformation (tension, compression, etc.).

q: 4. Torsion is produced in a beam due to
options: eccentricity of load from centroidal axis
explain: Torsion occurs when a load is applied at a distance (eccentricity) from the longitudinal centroidal axis, creating a twisting moment.

q: 5. Permanent set is
options: the force which acts permanently on the body
the shape of the member just after completion of construction
ratio of Poisson's ratio to Young's Modulus
explain: Permanent set refers to the residual, irrecoverable deformation that remains in a material after the load causing it beyond the elastic limit has been removed.

q: 6. Hoop stress is
explain: In thin-walled cylinders under internal pressure, hoop stress acts along the circumference and is tensile in nature.

q: 7. The load on spring per unit deflection is called
explain: Stiffness is defined as the load required to produce unit deflection in a spring (k = W/δ).

q: 8. Stress in a beam due to simple bending, is
explain: From the flexure formula σ = My/I, stress varies directly (linearly) proportional to the distance y from the neutral axis.

q: 9. For keeping the stress wholly compressive the load may be applied on a circular column anywhere within a concentric circle of diameter
explain: For a circular column of diameter d, the core (no-tension zone) is a concentric circle of diameter d/4, within which the eccentric load keeps stress wholly compressive.

q: 10. In a stressed body the maximum normal stress at any point is always
options: average of maximum and minimum shear stresses
sum of the two normal stresses acting in two principal directions
explain: By definition, a principal stress is the extreme (maximum or minimum) normal stress on any plane through the point with zero shear stress; hence the maximum normal stress is always a principal stress.

q: 11. Strain rosetters are used to
explain: Strain rosettes consist of multiple strain gauges arranged to measure linear (normal) strains in different directions at a point, from which principal strains can be derived.

q: 12. The ratio of the stresses produced by a suddenly applied load and by a gradually applied load on a bar is
explain: A suddenly applied load produces twice the stress (and deflection) of the same load applied gradually, a classic impact-loading result.

q: 13. Maximum strain theory for the failure of material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The maximum strain theory of failure is also known as St. Venant's theory.

q: 14. Total strain energy theory for the failure of a material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The total strain energy theory of failure is also known as Haig's theory (Beltrami's theory).

q: 15. The percentage reduction in area of a member from a direct tension test indicates
explain: Percentage reduction in cross-sectional area at fracture, like percentage elongation, is a standard measure of ductility.

q: 16. Strain in concrete at zero stress is called :
explain: Creep is the time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained load, often continuing after stress is removed.

q: 17. In an I section almost all the shear force is taken by
options: half the depth of each flange
explain: In an I-section, due to its geometry, the thin web carries the vast majority (typically over 90%) of the total shear force, while the flanges carry very little.

q: 18. Glass will obey Hooke's law up to
explain: Being a brittle material with no distinct yield point, glass behaves elastically (obeying Hooke's law) right up until sudden fracture.

q: 19. A shaft is subjected to bending moment M and a torque T simultaneously. The ratio of the maximum bending stress to maximum shear stress developed in the shaft is
explain: Comparing bending stress (σ = 32M/πd³) to shear stress (τ = 16T/πd³) for a circular shaft gives a ratio σ/τ = 2M/T.

q: 20. Limit of proportionality depends upon
explain: The limit of proportionality (where Hooke's law ceases to apply) is an intrinsic material property, depending on the type of material rather than its geometry or loading type.

q: 21. A close coil helical spring when subjected to a moment M having its axis along the axis of helix is
options: it is subjected to pure bending
its number of coil will increase
explain: When a closed-coil spring is subjected to a moment about its own (helix) axis, the wire experiences pure bending (as opposed to axial loading which causes torsion).

q: 22. The stress below which a material has a high probability of not failing under reversal of stress is known as
explain: The endurance limit (fatigue limit) is defined as the maximum stress below which a material can withstand an infinite number of stress reversals (cycles) without fatigue failure.

q: 23. In a rectangular shaft subjected to torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at
explain: For a rectangular (non-circular) shaft under torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at the midpoint of the longer side, per membrane analogy/torsion theory for non-circular sections.

q: 24. The specimen in Charpy impact test is supported as a
explain: In the Charpy impact test, the notched specimen is supported horizontally at both ends (as a simply supported beam) and struck at the center opposite the notch.

q: 25. How does the elastic limit vary with increase in temperature?
explain: As temperature increases, most metals soften and their elastic limit (and generally strength properties) decrease.

q: 26. Within the elastic range of a tensile test the deviation from Hooke's law and some after effect may be noticed. This is due to
options: material does not at all obey hooke's law
elastic limit is greater than ultimate strength
explain: Minor deviations and after-effects within the nominally elastic range are typically attributed to thermo-elastic effects (temperature changes accompanying rapid elastic deformation).

q: 27. The torsional rigidity of a shafts given by
explain: Torsional rigidity is defined as the torque required to produce a unit angle of twist, given by T/φ (equivalently GJ).
